title: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
objectives: Use int, float, complex and Decimal appropriately and explain floating-point error.
Slice strings with start, stop and step, including negative indices.
Format output with f-strings and format specifiers.
Apply common string methods: split, join, strip, replace, find, startswith, upper and title.
Explain why strings are immutable and why ''.join is preferred over += in loops.
definition: Python's numeric types are int (arbitrary precision integers), float (64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating point) and complex, with Decimal and Fraction available in the standard library for exact arithmetic. A str is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters that supports indexing, slicing, a rich set of methods and formatted string literals (f-strings).

theory.heading: Numbers: int, float, Decimal
theory.body: Python ints never overflow: 2 ** 100 is computed exactly because ints grow as needed. Floats are binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 and equality tests on floats are unreliable. For money, store whole paise or cents as ints, or use decimal.Decimal built from strings. Compare floats with math.isclose. Division / always returns a float, // performs floor division and round() uses banker's rounding (round half to even), so round(2.5) is 2.
points: int: unlimited size; float: about 15-17 significant digits.
Decimal('0.1') is exact; Decimal(0.1) inherits the float's error.
int('42'), float('3.5') and str(7) convert explicitly; int('3.5') raises ValueError.

theory.heading: Indexing and slicing
theory.body: Strings are sequences, so s[i] returns one character and negative indices count from the end (s[-1] is the last character). A slice s[start:stop:step] returns a new string from start up to but not including stop. Missing values default to the beginning, end and step 1, and out-of-range slice bounds are clipped instead of raising errors. s[::-1] reverses a string, a common interview one-liner for palindrome checks.
points: s[0:3] or s[:3]: first three characters.
s[10] on a short string raises IndexError, but s[10:20] returns ''.

theory.heading: Immutability and efficient building
theory.body: Strings cannot be changed in place: s[0] = 'J' raises TypeError, and every method such as upper() or replace() returns a new string. Building a large string with += in a loop can create many intermediate strings, which is quadratic in the worst case. Collect pieces in a list and call ''.join(pieces) once; it computes the total length and copies each piece only once.
points: Methods return new strings; assign the result: s = s.strip().
Use sep.join(iterable_of_strings) to concatenate many parts.
Immutability makes strings hashable, so they can be dictionary keys.

theory.heading: Essential string methods
theory.body: Most text processing in interviews uses a small set of methods. split() without arguments splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty strings, while split(',') splits on every comma exactly. strip() removes surrounding whitespace, find() returns -1 when not found whereas index() raises ValueError, and in tests substring membership.
points: Cleaning: strip, lstrip, rstrip, lower, upper, title, casefold.
Searching: in, find, index, count, startswith, endswith.
Transforming: replace, split, join, zfill, center.

theory.heading: Formatting output with f-strings
theory.body: f-strings (Python 3.6+) evaluate expressions inside braces at run time and accept a format specifier after a colon: {value:<width}, {value:>width}, {value:^width} for alignment, {value:.2f} for fixed decimals, {value:,} for thousands separators, {value:05d} for zero padding and {value:%} for percentages. Python 3.8 added the debugging form {x=}, which prints both the expression and its value.
points: Older styles: '%s' % x and '{}'.format(x) still appear in legacy code.

example.title: Cleaning and formatting a user record
example.body: Raw input often has stray spaces and inconsistent case. Chaining methods cleans it, slicing extracts parts and an f-string produces aligned output.

code.source:
raw = '   priya SHARMA , 9876543210 '
name, phone = [part.strip() for part in raw.split(',')]
name = name.title()                # 'Priya Sharma'
masked = '*' * 6 + phone[-4:]      # '******3210'
print(f'{name:<15}|{masked:>12}|')
print(f'{0.1 + 0.2 = }')            # debugging specifier (3.8+)
print(round(2.5), round(3.5))       # 2 4  (round half to even)

demonstration.description: Explore slicing, immutability and float behaviour in one short script.

code.source:
s = 'interview'
print(s[2:5], s[-3:], s[::-1])
print(s.upper(), s.count('i'), s.find('view'))
try:
    s[0] = 'I'
except TypeError as e:
    print('TypeError:', e)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(2 ** 70)
print(f'{1234567.891:,.2f}')

takeaways: ints have unlimited precision; floats are approximate, so compare them with math.isclose.
Use integer paise/cents or Decimal for money.
Slices exclude the stop index, accept negative indices and never raise IndexError.
Strings are immutable; methods return new strings.
Join many pieces with ''.join(list) instead of += in a loop.
f-strings with format specifiers handle alignment, decimals and separators.

interview.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in Python?
interview.answer: Floats are stored in binary, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with math.isclose, or use Decimal or integers for exact values.
interview.explanation: Mention that this is IEEE 754 behaviour shared by most languages, not a Python bug.

interview.question: How do you reverse a string in Python?
interview.answer: Use slicing with a step of -1: s[::-1]. Alternatively ''.join(reversed(s)).
interview.explanation: Interviewers often follow up with a palindrome check: s == s[::-1], possibly after normalising case and removing non-alphanumeric characters.

interview.question: Why are strings immutable, and what are the consequences?
interview.answer: Immutability lets strings be hashed and used as dict keys and set members, makes them safe to share between names and threads, and enables interning. The consequence is that every modification creates a new string, so repeated += in a loop is inefficient compared with ''.join.
interview.explanation: Linking immutability to hashability and performance shows depth.

interview.question: What is the difference between str.find and str.index?
interview.answer: Both return the lowest index of a substring. find returns -1 when it is not found; index raises ValueError.
interview.explanation: Choose find when absence is normal, index when absence is an error you want surfaced.

interview.question: What does round(2.5) return, and why?
interview.answer: 2. Python 3 uses round half to even (banker's rounding), so .5 cases round to the nearest even number. This reduces bias when many values are rounded. For commercial rounding use Decimal.quantize with ROUND_HALF_UP.
interview.explanation: A surprising-output question that tests attention to numeric details.

practice.title: Aligned invoice formatter
practice.objective: Combine string methods, integer arithmetic for money and f-string alignment to produce a clean report.
practice.statement: Read invoice lines of the form item_name quantity unit_price. Item names use underscores instead of spaces and may have any case. For each line print the item name with underscores replaced by spaces in title case, left-aligned in 14 characters, then the quantity right-aligned in 4 characters, then the line amount right-aligned in 10 characters with exactly two decimals. Finally print TOTAL left-aligned in 18 characters followed by the grand total right-aligned in 10 characters. To avoid floating-point error, convert prices to integer paise before multiplying.
practice.input_format: The first line is N. Each of the next N lines is 'name quantity price' where price has at most two decimals.
practice.output_format: N item lines followed by one TOTAL line, formatted as described.
constraints: Prices are non-negative with at most two decimal places.
Format money as rupees.paise with exactly two digits after the point.

quiz.question: What does this slicing example print?
quiz.explanation: Index 2 is 't'; the slice stops before index 5, giving 'ter'. s[-3:] takes the last three characters, 'iew'.

quiz.question: What does this round() example print?
quiz.explanation: Python 3 rounds halves to the nearest even integer: 2.5 -> 2 and 3.5 -> 4.

quiz.question: What does this f-string formatting print?
quiz.explanation: .2f gives two decimal places; 05d pads the integer with zeros to width 5.

quiz.question: You build a 100,000-line CSV report by doing report += line inside a loop. A reviewer asks for a change. What is the better approach?
options: Append lines to a list and call ''.join(lines) once at the end
Use report = report + line instead of +=
Use a global variable for the report
Convert each line to bytes before adding it
quiz.explanation: Strings are immutable, so repeated concatenation may copy the growing string many times. join builds the result in a single pass.

quiz.question: name = 'ravi'. Which statement raises an error?
quiz.explanation: Strings are immutable, so item assignment raises TypeError. Slicing past the end returns an empty string rather than raising.
